title: The thirst
hookLine: the second truth: suffering comes with craving (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)

cards: Drink salt water and you get thirstier. The very thing you reach for to fix the thirst feeds it. Other things work a bit like that.
One more episode, and the next one starts on its own. One more look at the phone. One more thing in the cart.
Each one is supposed to settle it, and each leaves the wanting a little wider. After it names suffering, the Buddha's first teaching names where suffering comes from, with a word for thirst.

teach.b: First, the word. In Pali it's tanha, and the Pali-English Dictionary glosses it as thirst, and as craving: the same word does for a dry throat and a restless mind.

Second, now here, now there. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the second noble truth says suffering arises with craving, bound up with delight and passion, seeking delight now here, now there. That's its restlessness.
It doesn't settle on one thing and rest. It finishes one glass and looks for the next.
Third, three thirsts. The same teaching names three kinds. A thirst for sense pleasures: tastes, sounds, touch, the good things.
A thirst for being: to become something, to last, to be someone. And a thirst for not being: for something to stop, to go away, not to exist. That third one is easy to miss.
Pushing away can be thirst, too. Wanting the feeling gone, the person gone, the day over, has the same dry, reaching quality as wanting more.

Fourth, not every wish. Tanha doesn't mean wanting anything at all. The Buddha's own path asks for effort, and when a teaching on right effort describes the wish for wholesome states, it uses a different word, chanda.
That wish isn't called thirst. The thirst is the grasping kind of wanting: the kind that can't stand still, and never quite says enough.

how: Buddhists study the second noble truth as part of the four noble truths, and in meditation practice noticing craving as it arises, without acting on it or suppressing it.

o: the plain ache a body feels when it lacks water
thirst, the craving the Buddha names as suffering's source
a sudden hunger that comes after a long day of fasting

games.q: the three thirsts — tap the pairs.

s: tanha means every wish of any kind
the path itself asks for a wish to do what's wholesome; the texts call that chanda.
the second truth names three kinds of craving
for sense pleasures, for being, and for not being.
wanting something to go away can't be craving
craving for not being is one of the three.

games.q: you're sitting still, and a strong pull arrives to get up and check your phone. what does today's practice ask?
o: feed it quickly so it goes away
watch it like thirst, without feeding or fighting
games.why: feeding the thirst is the salt water. the practice is to look at it, where it sits in the body, and see what it does unfed.

practice: Sit still, and before long a pull will turn up: to check something, to move, to make this end. Don't feed it and don't fight it; look at it like thirst, noticing where it sits in the body, the chest, the hands, the jaw.
Then stay, and watch what it does when it isn't fed.

wordCard.voice: Tanha: Pali for thirst, the craving the second noble truth names as where suffering comes from. For pleasure, for being, and for not being. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: thirst, craving. The Sanskrit form is tṛṣṇā.

carryVoice: Your line: now here, now there. Not every wish is thirst; the grasping kind is. Day seven hundred two.
